title: An exact solution tests the solver; a penalization parameter sweep tests how fast an approximate model approaches a reference, and the best setting may not be the largest
summary: Three checks of the same low-Reynolds-number solver: a pipe profile against the exact parabola, a channel with a Brinkman friction term against its closed-form solution for four friction values, and a Brinkman-penalised solid against a mesh that follows the body. Read each for what it is compared against and which error is controlled by which knob.

media.alt: Two panels against Brinkman friction alpha from 1 to 1e10 on log axes, for two mesh sizes. Left: mean speed leaking inside the penalised disk falls from about 1 metre per second at alpha = 1 to about 5e-7 on the coarser mesh and 2e-8 on the finer mesh at alpha = 1e10. Right: the percentage velocity mismatch outside the penalised region falls from about 65 percent to a minimum near 1 percent, marked by a star at alpha of 1e4 on the coarse mesh and 1e6 on the fine mesh, then rises again to about 7 and 2 percent.

03_mfv_a6_pipe_flow_spotcheck: 3D pipe flow compared with the exact Hagen-Poiseuille profile
source.note: The page teaches the generic reading of an exact-solution check and of a penalization-parameter sweep using standard theory (Hagen-Poiseuille flow, the Brinkman channel solution). Numbers quoted are printed on the figures or reproduced by the Apply script; the viscosity needed for the Brinkman check is an assumption stated there. The cfdcore project holds similar figures with its own explainer.

read_the_figure.question: Does the computed flow equal a solution known in closed form, and as a friction penalty is made stiffer, does an immersed solid behave like a real wall on a mesh that follows the body, and at what price?
read_the_figure.axes: Pipe: x is r/R from axis to wall, y is u/u_max; the grey curve is the exact parabola, blue dots are three computed values. Brinkman channel: x is position y across a 20 micrometre gap (from -10 to 10 micrometres), y is velocity in m/s; one curve per friction value alpha. Penalisation sweep: x is the friction alpha on a log axis from 1 to 1e10 in Pa s per square metre; left y is the mean speed inside the penalised disk on a log axis, right y is the mean relative velocity mismatch outside it in percent; one line per mesh size, stars mark each minimum.
look_at: Pipe: the three dots lie on the grey curve at r/R of 0, 0.5 and 0.9; the label gives a maximum relative error of 2.7e-14.
Brinkman channel: the peak falls and the profile flattens as alpha rises; every curve is zero at both walls.
Sweep, left: both lines fall with alpha; the finer mesh falls further. Compare the slope with -1, the leak speed one expects when friction balances a fixed driving force.
Sweep, right: mismatch drops steeply, reaches a minimum near 1 percent and rises again; the two stars sit at different alpha and the finer mesh has the lower minimum.
Titles of the right panel overlap its y label and the heading is crowded.
read_the_figure.proves: The pipe check shows the discretisation reproduces a profile it can represent exactly. The Brinkman channel check shows the penalised equation is being solved correctly for four values of alpha. The sweep shows two competing errors: leakage shrinks monotonically with alpha while the discretisation error outside the solid grows once alpha is large for the mesh, so a mesh-dependent best alpha exists.
if_wrong: Pipe error far above round-off for a profile in the discrete space: mapping or boundary-condition error.
Brinkman peak not falling with alpha, or non-zero wall values: friction term missing or applied in the wrong region.
Leakage that stops falling at large alpha: a floor from solver tolerance or conditioning.
Mismatch that decreases forever with alpha on a fixed mesh: not seen here, but would suggest the sweep ended before the conditioning limit.
must_check: The comparison solution is exact or independent, and its formulation is the same equation.
The viscosity, driving force and geometry needed to reproduce the exact curve are stated.
Both the error you want to be small (leakage) and the one that grows (outer mismatch) are plotted together.
The sweep is repeated on at least two meshes so a mesh dependence can be told from a physical one.
Minimum markers are drawn at the actual minimum, with the value printed.
as_drawn: Pipe: dots at r/R = 0, 0.5, 0.9 with u/u_max of 1, 0.75 and 0.19, which equal 1 - (r/R)^2: 1, 0.75, 0.19. Label: PASS, maximum relative error 2.7e-14.
Brinkman channel: curves for alpha = 0 (peak 0.005 m/s), 3e6 (about 0.00445), 1e7 (about 0.0035) and 5e7 (about 0.0016). Label: ODE residual below 1e-6 relative for all alpha.

Sweep, left, coarse mesh (lc = r_cyl/3): about 1.3 m/s at alpha = 1, 5.5e-3 at 1e4, 1.7e-4 at 1e6, 7e-6 at 1e8, 5e-7 at 1e10. Fine mesh (lc = r_cyl/6): from 5.5e-3 at 1e4 to 5.5e-5, 5.5e-7 and 2e-8 at 1e6, 1e8 and 1e10.

Sweep, right: about 65 percent at alpha = 1, 27 at 100, then near 1.5 percent at 1e4. Footnote: minimum 1.04 percent at alpha = 1e6 on the fine mesh, 1.46 percent at 1e4 on the coarse mesh. At 1e10 the coarse mesh is near 7 percent and the fine mesh near 2 percent.

terms.meaning: Steady laminar flow in a long pipe driven by a pressure gradient; the velocity profile is a parabola, zero at the wall.
A term proportional to velocity added to the momentum equation. Large values slow the fluid to a halt, so a region carrying it behaves like a porous or solid body.
Representing a solid body on a fixed mesh by switching on a large Brinkman friction inside it, instead of cutting the mesh to the body's boundary.
A mesh whose cell faces follow the boundary of the body; the reference against which a penalised solution is compared.
The residual fluid speed inside the region that is supposed to be solid.
How sensitive the discrete solution is to small errors; a very stiff friction term makes the local system poorly conditioned on a fixed mesh.
Agreement to near the rounding limit of double-precision arithmetic, about 1e-16 relative.

remember: Agreement with an exact solution to round-off means the discrete problem is solved exactly, which is expected when the exact solution lies in the discrete space.
A penalised solid leaks; the leak shrinks as friction grows, roughly like one over alpha.
Two errors that trade off give a U-shaped curve and a best setting, not a monotone one.
If the best setting moves with the mesh, tie the parameter to the mesh size, do not fix it.
An exact solution must be reproduced with the same parameters, so state the viscosity and force.

understand.title: Why the pipe error can sit at 1e-14
understand.text: The exact profile is a quadratic. If the velocity space contains quadratics, as many stable Stokes element pairs do, the exact solution is representable and the discrete solution equals it up to solver tolerance. A tiny error is therefore the expected outcome, and a test of the whole pipeline (geometry, mapping, boundary conditions, solver) at once. The element used is not stated in the figure.

understand.title: What the Brinkman friction does to a channel
understand.text: With friction the profile is no longer a parabola but a hyperbolic cosine: the fluid is held back everywhere, the peak falls, and the profile flattens in the core with a thin layer near the walls. The layer thickness is one over kappa, where kappa is the square root of friction over viscosity. In the figure alpha = 5e7 gives a layer of about 4.5 micrometres in a 10 micrometre half-gap, so the profile is flatter but not yet a plug.

understand.title: Two errors, two knobs
understand.text: Leakage is a modelling error of the penalised formulation and falls as alpha grows. The mismatch outside the body also contains a discretisation error: a very large friction makes the local system stiff on a mesh that cannot resolve the thin layer it creates, so the outer flow gets worse. A finer mesh moves the minimum to a larger alpha and lowers it, which is what the stars show.

understand.title: Reading minima on a log axis
understand.text: The minimum is shallow and sits between points a hundredfold apart in alpha. The star marks the lowest measured point, not a fitted minimum, so the best alpha is known only to the grid of values tried.

steps.title: Hagen-Poiseuille profile
steps.note: From the axisymmetric Stokes equation for a pressure gradient G. The three dots give 1, 0.75 and 0.19.

steps.title: Brinkman channel equation
steps.note: Steady unidirectional flow between plates at y = -h and y = h with driving force G per volume. Setting alpha to zero gives plain Poiseuille flow.

steps.title: Closed-form solution
steps.note: Peak at y = 0. For kappa h much smaller than 1 it reduces to G(h^2 - y^2)/(2 mu); for large kappa h it approaches G/alpha in the core.

steps.title: Peak relative to the unpenalised channel
steps.note: A one-number comparison for each curve. Worked in Apply, with the viscosity assumption stated.

steps.title: Expected leak scaling
steps.note: Where friction balances a fixed driving force the speed falls like one over alpha. The fine-mesh line has slope about -1 between alpha = 1e4 and 1e8; the coarse-mesh line is shallower, about -0.7.

steps.title: Mismatch as a sum of two errors
steps.note: A schematic decomposition, not a fitted law: the first term falls with alpha, the second grows with alpha and shrinks with h, so the minimum moves right and down on refinement.

worked.title: Do the drawn Brinkman peaks follow the closed form?
worked.problem: The unpenalised peak in the figure is 0.005 m/s in a gap from -10 to 10 micrometres. The viscosity is not printed; assume 1e-3 Pa s. What peak does the closed form give for alpha = 1e7, and does it match the drawn curve?

solution.text: Find kappa h for the half-gap h = 1e-5 m.
Peak ratio from the closed form.

worked.answer: About 3.5e-3 m/s, which is the drawn orange peak. The same calculation gives 4.4e-3 for alpha = 3e6 and 1.58e-3 for alpha = 5e7, both matching the figure, so the assumed viscosity of 1e-3 Pa s reproduces all three curves.

analyze.q: The fine-mesh leak line has slope about -1 up to alpha = 1e8 and then flattens, and the coarse-mesh line is shallower throughout. What does each say about what limits the leak?
analyze.hint: Compare with the expected slope of -1.

analyze.q: On the right panel the two lines coincide at alpha = 1e4 and then separate. What does separation tell you about which error dominates at small and large alpha?
analyze.hint: Model error should not depend on the mesh.

analyze.q: The profile at alpha = 5e7 is described in the title as approaching a plug with a thin wall layer. Using kappa h, how much of that description holds?
analyze.hint: Compute kappa h and compare the layer thickness 1/kappa with the half-gap.

evaluate.q: A reader proposes using the largest alpha tested because leakage is smallest. Using the right panel, what do you advise?
evaluate.hint: Which quantity is the outer flow, and where is its minimum?

evaluate.q: The pipe check reaches 2.7e-14 and the penalisation check bottoms at about 1 percent. Do both count as passes, and what does each pass certify?
evaluate.hint: Exact representable solution versus an approximate model.

create: Design a mesh-coupled friction rule alpha(h) from the two stars, and say which extra mesh sizes and what plot would test it.
Sketch a three-panel figure that puts the exact Brinkman curves, their numerical counterparts and the residual of each on one scale, so a reader can see both agreement and error.

checks.q: Why is a relative error of 2.7e-14 against the exact pipe profile not surprising?
checks.hint: What does the velocity space contain?
checks.answer: The exact profile is quadratic and representable in the discrete space, so the solution equals it up to round-off and solver tolerance.

checks.q: For the Brinkman channel, what is kappa h for alpha = 3e6 with viscosity 1e-3 Pa s and h = 10 micrometres?
checks.hint: kappa is the square root of alpha over mu.

checks.q: Leakage keeps falling with alpha but the outer mismatch rises beyond a minimum. Why?
checks.hint: Think of a model error and a discretisation error.
checks.answer: The model error falls with alpha; a very stiff friction term makes the local discrete system ill-conditioned on a fixed mesh, so the discretisation error grows.

checks.q: The minimum mismatch moves from alpha = 1e4 to 1e6 when the mesh is refined. What follows for a design run?
checks.answer: The best alpha depends on resolution, so alpha should be raised in step with mesh refinement, not fixed at the largest value.

checks.q: How would you check that the minimum is not a plotting artefact of a coarse alpha grid?
checks.answer: Add alpha values between 1e3 and 1e8 on both meshes, report the lowest measured point and its mismatch, and see whether it stays in the same decade.

provenance.notes: Disclosure: the images carry PASS and FINDING banners, internal names (a solver function in the pipe legend, an automatic-differentiation checker in the Brinkman banner, milestone prefixes A.6 and D.1/D.2 in titles and filenames, mesh-size parameter names lc and r_cyl, and the phrase 'the equation topology optimization actually solves'), and the sweep footnote refers to a future topology-optimisation run and to literature on continuation schemes. None are repeated; the page teaches the generic reading. Owner review: (1) the right panel of the penalisation figure has its title overlapping the y label and the FINDING heading, a layout defect. (2) The Brinkman title says the profile becomes 'plug-with-thin-wall-layer'; at the largest alpha drawn the layer is about 4.5 micrometres in a 10 micrometre half-gap (viscosity 1e-3 Pa s assumed, not printed), so the curve is flatter but not a plug. (3) The Brinkman peaks match the closed form only for an assumed viscosity of 1e-3 Pa s; state it on the figure. (4) The pipe check plots three points only. (5) The sweep leak footnote does not say whether the penalised region is the same size on both meshes.
